title: Nouns: gender
content: Middle Egyptian nouns have grammatical gender. A frequent feminine marker is -t, although not every final t is simply a gender ending and spelling can vary.

quiz.q: Which form is feminine in the pair sꜣ / sꜣt?

title: Nouns: singular, dual and plural
content: Egyptian distinguishes singular, dual and plural. Plural morphology commonly involves -w and feminine plural patterns can involve -wt. Dual forms have their own endings. Written number marking can interact with plural strokes and determinatives.

quiz.q: Which ending frequently marks a masculine plural?

title: Adjectives and agreement
content: Attributive adjectives commonly follow the nouns they describe and agree in gender and number. This is different from ordinary English adjective order and often feels more familiar to speakers of languages with post-nominal description.

quiz.q: In pr nfr, which word comes first?

title: Independent pronouns
objectives: Use jnk, ntk, ntf and related forms
content: Independent pronouns are used especially in nominal and emphasized constructions. Learn them as complete lexical items rather than trying to derive them from English pronouns.

title: Suffix pronouns
content: Suffix pronouns attach to nouns, prepositions and many verb forms. Core forms include .j 'my/I', .k 'your/you' masculine singular, .ṯ 'your/you' feminine singular, .f 'his/he', .s 'her/she', .n 'our/we', .ṯn 'your/you plural' and .sn 'their/they'.

quiz.q: What does the suffix .f usually mark?

title: Possession and the genitive
objectives: Use n as a genitival linker
content: Possession can be expressed by direct juxtaposition or with genitival constructions. Literal word order often differs from English. Suffix pronouns also provide very compact possession.

quiz.q: Which small word can link 'house' and 'king' in a genitive construction?

title: Prepositions
objectives: Use m, r, n, ḥr and ẖr
content: Prepositions are frequent and multifunctional. m may mean in/with/as; r may mean to/toward/at/concerning; n may mean to/for; ḥr often means on/upon; ẖr means under. Translate the construction, not an isolated gloss.
